blocks.text: Stephanie Fagadau : Where the Image Begins

Stephanie Fagadau ’s photography is less concerned with documenting reality than testing its limits. Her images emerge in the uncertain space between what is seen and what is perceived: a body reduced to a surface, light transformed into matter, a fragment acquiring a life of its own. What remains is not simply the subject before the camera, but everything the image manages to set in motion memory, sensation, suggestion, sometimes even unease.

At the heart of Fagadau’s practice lies a fascination with the fragile boundary between presence and disappearance. She does not approach the world as something to be faithfully described, but as something to be looked at, experienced and reconfigured through the act of photography. Her gaze isolates, obscures and displaces. A reflection may become more significant than the figure it conceals; a shadow may carry more weight than the object that casts it. Nothing is quite where we expect it to be.

This is where the particular strength of her work resides. She allows ambiguity to remain active within the image. Rather than offering an immediate reading, her photographs slow down perception. They ask us to look again to reconsider what initially appeared obvious, and to notice what happens at the margins of the frame. Her affinity with photographers such as Vivian Maier, Robert Doisneau, Marc Riboud and, above all, Saul Leiter is revealing. Like Leiter, she understands that an image does not necessarily become more powerful by making its subject more visible. Blur, reflections, colour, obstruction and fragments can sometimes bring us closer to a subject precisely by keeping part of it out of reach. For Stephanie Fagadau, photography remains fundamentally an act of looking. Technique matters, but only insofar as it serves emotion. The decisive moment is not necessarily spectacular; it may be almost imperceptible a gesture, a gaze, a trace of time, a fleeting encounter on a street. Her practice is built on this attentiveness to what might otherwise pass unnoticed. There is also, throughout her work, a persistent question of memory. The photograph preserves an instant, but it does more than simply keep a record of it. It transforms the instant into something that can be revisited, reinterpreted and felt differently over time. In that sense, her photographs occupy a space between evidence and imagination, between what happened and what the image allows us to remember. Her transition from theatre to photography is therefore more than a change of medium. It marks a shift from directing what happens before an audience to responding to what happens before her eyes. The camera becomes a way of remaining open to the unexpected. What ultimately distinguishes Stéphanie Fagadau’s approach is this refusal to force the image into a conclusion. She photographs in order to discover rather than to confirm. Between clarity and mystery, colour and silence, presence and absence, her work reminds us that seeing is never a passive act. A photograph does not simply show us something. At its best, it challenges the eye.

What was your first photographic breakthrough? S.F.: I honestly believe my photographic breakthrough came during Covid. My theatre was closed, and I felt the need to keep creating, but in a different way. That was when I turned to photography, an art form I have always deeply loved.

A photographic memory from your childhood? S.F.: When my mother died, I found some old negatives and had them developed. Among them was a photograph of the three of us. I have absolutely no idea who took it. I was about seven years old, sitting on my mother’s lap, with my father beside us, and the three of us radiated an incredible sense of joy. That is the image and the memory I want to keep.

The camera from your childhood? S.F.: My only memory of a camera from my childhood is my mother’s. She had an old Kodak that made a very distinctive, rather intense sound every time she took a picture. Strangely enough, I can still hear that sound in my head today.

The one you use today? S.F.: I mainly photograph with two cameras that I am very attached to: the Nikon Z50 and the Fujifilm X100. I also take some of my pictures with my iPhone, when I see something really worth photographing and don’t have a camera with me.
The man or woman in photography who has inspired you? S.F.: Without a doubt, Vivian Maier and Saul Leiter. They are my two great photographic loves.

An image you wish you had taken? S.F.: That’s a difficult question, because there are so many. But probably The Kiss by the Hôtel de Ville by Robert Doisneau. Even though it was staged, it remains a mythical image for me, a true landmark of street photography, with a poetry that has endured through time.
The one that has moved you the most? S.F.: The napalm Girl , taken during the Vietnam War. Every time I see that picture, it moves me profoundly. It triggers an almost uncontrollable emotion in me.

And the one that made you angry? S.F.: Honestly, there isn’t one particular image. But whenever I see photographs in which human beings are degraded or humiliated, and we are forced to witness something terrible without being able to do anything about it, it makes me deeply angry.

Which photograph changed the world? S.F.: I would so love photography to be able to change the world, or at least profoundly change the way people see it. Unfortunately, I feel that an image can create a shock, awaken consciences in the moment, but that it is not enough to permanently transform the world we live in. I am thinking in particular of the photograph taken in 2015 by Nilufer Demir, showing the young Syrian refugee Alan Kurdi, found dead on a Turkish beach. That image shook people’s consciences. I wish it had changed the course of our history even more.

And which photograph changed your world? S.F.: It didn’t literally change my world, but it represents exactly what I want to seek in photography: The Ultimate Confrontation by Marc Riboud, taken in 1967 during a demonstration against the Vietnam War. This young pacifist woman holding out a flower in front of the weapons brings together everything I love in an image: telling a story, provoking emotion, making us think, but also leaving room for dreams and imagination.

A key image in your personal pantheon? S.F.: I don’t think there is just one. There is the entire universe of Saul Leiter. His photographs made me understand that blur, textures, reflections and the things that sometimes conceal the subject can, paradoxically, allow us to see it more clearly. In the way he worked with colour, you can feel how deeply he was influenced by painting and by Abstract Expressionism. I find his work to be pure poetry.
What interests you most in an image? S.F.: The emotion it gives me.
What details do you look for in a face, a landscape or an object? S.F.: Traces of time.

Elliott Erwitt said: “Colour is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree? S.F.: Not entirely. I think colour can be just as interpretive as black and white. In Saul Leiter’s work, for example, colour doesn’t simply describe reality: it transforms it. For me, they are simply two different ways of telling an image.

Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? S.F.: For me, technique serves emotion. It allows you to go further, but it can never replace the eye. Some photographs are technically perfect and yet provoke nothing, while others, which may be more imperfect, can generate a very powerful emotion. The two are complementary, but emotion remains paramount.

Is beauty in photography purely aesthetic for you? S.F.: Absolutely not. Beauty can be found in the tiniest detail, in a look, a reflection, a colour. It doesn’t have to be perfect, or even obvious. In photography, beauty is everywhere; you simply have to know how to see it.
What can make silence visible in a photograph? S.F.: I think silence can be made visible through a gaze. Sometimes a look says much more than words.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Can a photograph be truer than reality? S.F.: Any photograph can transform reality and, in a sense, transcend it. But what I prefer is to capture a present moment, that unique instant which we manage to seize and which will probably never exist in quite the same way again.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event? S.F.: Change our perception, I’m not sure. But photography is a witness to an event. It allows us to preserve a trace of it, to engrave it in our memory.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? S.F.: It can be both. A photograph is a testimony because it preserves the trace of a moment, but it can also be a form of manipulation: through framing, staging or transforming the image, we can direct reality and make it tell another story.
What makes a good photograph? S.F.: Finding the right moment—the one that tells us something.
What quality is essential to being a good photographer? S.F.: Knowing how to look.
How do you choose your projects? S.F.: With my heart. It may sound like an easy answer, but that is genuinely how I work.

How would you describe your creative process? S.F.: My process is quite instinctive: looking, remaining attentive to what is happening, and trying to capture the right moment. Then being demanding of my own work and continuing to learn, always.
An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart? S.F.: The publication of my photography book in 2027, and finally taking the time to organise my exhibition.
The person you would like to photograph? S.F.: I would love to photograph Meryl Streep. She is one of the people I admire most.
And the person you would like to be photographed by? S.F.: Annie Leibovitz, without a doubt.

One indispensable photography book? S.F.: There are so many… I mainly believe that we have to find the books that are indispensable to us personally, the ones that nourish our own way of seeing. But if I had to choose one, it would be The Unseen Saul Leiter , a book I can look at again and again without ever tiring of it.
What was the last photograph you took? S.F.: At the very moment I am answering this question, it is a photograph of a man on a bus, reading his newspaper.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook or TikTok—and why? S.F.: Instagram, without hesitation. Facebook a little, TikTok not at all. Instagram remains, for me, the social network of images, the one that best corresponds to photography and to the way I like to share my work.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? S.F.: The possibility of showing your work to a much wider audience, almost without borders. Today, a photograph can be seen anywhere in the world within seconds. But social media has also accelerated the way we look at images: we see an enormous number of them, sometimes without really taking the time to look.
One Instagram account everyone should follow? S.F.: There are so many… But I still feel like saying mine!

What is your view on AI? S.F.: It’s a vast and rather delicate subject. AI now allows us to retouch photographs much more easily and save an enormous amount of time. Personally, I like retouching my images, but I don’t like transforming them: what I show remains what I actually photographed. That sense of honesty is important to me in my work. But everyone is free to make their own choices, and I’m not here to judge anyone else’s.

Colour or black and white? S.F.: Impossible to choose; I genuinely work with both. I tend to favour black and white for portraits because I find that it particularly emphasises emotions and expressions. But I also love colour for all the richness and freedom it can offer. They are two different languages, and I have no desire to give either one up.

Natural or artificial light? S.F.: Natural light, without hesitation. Even for portraits, I like working in places where people feel comfortable and composing with whatever light is already there. It’s also a little challenge I enjoy giving myself. I admire photographers who have mastered artificial light and studio photography perfectly, but that simply isn’t what drives me.

Which city do you find the most photogenic? S.F.: New York, of course. Every neighbourhood, every street can become a film set. It offers an incredible wealth of photographic material. More broadly, travelling forces us to look differently. I obviously haven’t seen everything, but New York remains a high point for me.
The city, country or culture you dream of discovering? S.F.: Japan. It is really the next major trip I would like to take. I want to discover the country, its culture and its colours.

The place you never get tired of? S.F.: Paris, the city where I live. Since I started practising street photography, I have learned to look at it differently and rediscover it again and again. And then Rome, the other city where I could imagine living. I could go back there over and over, always with the same joy of being there.

The image that represents the state of the world today for you? S.F.: I don’t know if it represents the state of the world on its own, but it certainly tells part of the story. It is a photograph by Maximilien Lamy, taken in Lacanau, showing a couple sitting on sun loungers on the beach while, in the distance, fires are ravaging the landscape. That image deeply affected me. It tells the story both of a burning earth and of a form of passivity in the face of what is happening before our eyes.
What do you think is missing from the world today? S.F.: Kindness.
If God existed, would you ask Him to pose for you, or would you opt for a selfie? S.F.: Obviously, I would ask Him to pose for me. Photographing God would be pretty hard to turn down!
Your favourite drug? S.F.: The smell of my children. And unfortunately, sugar too!
Your best way to disconnect? S.F.: Taking my camera, going for a walk and having no idea what awaits me. That is my best way of letting go, almost like an antidepressant.

Your latest act of madness? S.F.: I don’t know if it was madness, but it was a real tsunami in my life. A few months ago, I sold my theatre, the Théâtre de la Comédie des Champs-Élysées, which I had run for twenty years. Making such a decision at fifty, especially as a woman, is not insignificant. But I have absolutely no regrets. In fact, I think it is one of the most beautiful acts of madness I have ever committed for my own well-being.

Your greatest professional extravagance? S.F.: Taking a new professional direction at fifty. I don’t really like talking about a “new career”, but rather a new stage in life. And ultimately, I’m quite proud of it.
The job you would never have wanted to do? S.F.: A job that would make me unhappy.
Which question throws you off balance the most? S.F.: The one I don’t know how to answer.
The last thing you did for the first time? S.F.: Answer this question… and realise that I have absolutely no idea!
Your greatest regret? S.F.: Not having expressed certain things enough to my parents, both of whom I have lost. I still had so much to tell them.
If you had to start all over again? S.F.: Oh no! Far too exhausting. I’m too old for that!

If I could organise your ideal dinner, who would be at the table? S.F.: The obvious answer would be a dinner with everyone I love, my children and my partner first and foremost. But if I were to imagine a dinner with people I would have dreamed of meeting, it would be a dinner of women: Michelle Obama, Simone Veil, Marie Curie, Meryl Streep and Jackie Kennedy. I think the atmosphere could be quite explosive!
What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? S.F.: That I did my best. Perhaps, in the end, that is what matters most.

The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? S.F.: That I am a generous person. I have dozens of flaws, but I know that I give a great deal without necessarily expecting anything in return—which has sometimes got me into trouble. But it is a quality I particularly value.
One last word? S.F.: Love yourselves.
Text and interview by Carole Schmitz
